newsitem.title: USA: Despite fuss, jobs survive U.S. minimum wage hike.
newsitem.headline: Despite fuss, jobs survive U.S. minimum wage hike.

text.p: Billed by detractors as a "cruel hoax" and "hurting those it's intended to help", the raise given to 4.2 million U.S. minimum wage workers last October has yet to trigger measurable job loss, economists said.

"Opponents argued with great vigor that if you raise the minimum wage, the sky would fall. It hasn't fallen a bit," said Jared Bernstein, a labor economist at the Economic Policy Institute in Washington D.C. and advocate for minimum wage legislation.

Bill Parks, an economist at the Bureau of Labor Statistics which takes no official stance regarding the minimum wage issue, said their jobs data showed little to no impact on unemployment after October 1, the day the minimum wage rose 50 cents to $4.75 per hour.
"Nothing jumped out at us. We pulled some series and looked at them informally and there was just no obvious impact in terms of disemployment effects," Parks said.

Economists concentrate on four subsets of BLS monthly employment data that have a high concentration of minimum wage workers: general merchandise stores, eating and drinking establishments, the employment of teenagers (16 to 19 years old) and the teenage labor force participation rate.
All four series showed no trend change after the wage hike, but Parks cautioned that on a monthly basis the figures "jump around" and analysis should be done on a trailing basis.
"I would caution that one should never place too much emphasis on a one month change for any labor market series," Parks said.
Opponents of the hike argued that a strong U.S. economy and tight labor market counterbalanced job losses and that the wage rise was so small the impact was hard to discern.

"Believe me, the (disemployment impact) of going from $4.25 to $4.75 and going from $4.25 to $20.00 is only different in magnitude," said Finis Welch, a professor at Texas A&M and an outspoken opponent of the minimum wage.

"The 'speak' that was coined in Princeton and used by the (Clinton) administration in these last rounds of debates -- that it is not clear an increase in the minimum wage produces unemployment -- all that means is if you make it small enough, it's hard to see," he added.

According to BLS statistics for 1995, only 3.3 percent of the 110.038 million U.S. wage and salary workers were paid the prevailing minimum wage or less. This has decreased from 5.8 percent in 1985 and 7.8 percent in 1979, when the data series began.

The 'new economic thought' that Welch was referring to was developed by Alan Krueger, a Princeton University professor and coauthor with David Card of "Myth and Measurement: The New Economics of the Minimum Wage".
Krueger told Reuters he did not see any reflection in the BLS employment data of the wage hike, but did see an almost instantaneous move higher in retail sector wages.
"It's hard to see any effect of it in the employment data. It would be frightening if this (tight labor market) was on top of a negative minimum wage effect," he said.

While discussing a dearth of publicity about the benign impact of the wage hike, Kruger said: "I think the reason why you haven't heard much about it is that it goes against the conventional wisdom that we would see job losses and we have not."
Wall Street economists said they saw no discernable impact in the data they typically analyze to stay abreast of the economy.

"It doesn't seem to me it has had any impact in the consumer price index (CPI), monthly employment, or the personal income and consumption numbers, either," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
"It should have impacted the CPI numbers more than it did," she added.

A second 40 cent leg of the minimum wage increase will take effect next September 1, lifting the pay floor to $5.15 per hour. Most economists expect little fallout from this second increase given its relatively small size and the robust U.S. economy.

The purchasing power of the minimum wage has dropped drastically since its inception on October 24, 1938 when President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Fair Labor Standards Act which established a minimum wage of 25 cents per hour, a maximum work week of 44 hours, and banned child labor.
At the time, 25 cents could buy three 12 ounce boxes of cornflakes, and a 10-pound sack of flour cost almost 40 cents.
The minimum wage had previously last been raised in 1991 to $4.25 per hour after a 10-year deadlock on the issue between Congress and the Reagan and Bush administrations.
According to the Labor Department, most minimum wage workers are harvesters, janitors, child care providers and employees in the retail and food service industries.
Four in ten minimum wage earners are the sole bread winners of their families.
"I would advocate for returning the minimum wage to its historical level in the late 70's...which would be closer to the low six-dollar level in today's dollars," Bernstein said.
((--N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1677))
